title: KV cache compaction improvements (allocator + eviction + scheduler contract)
creator: Talia Benson
description:
Umbrella project for reducing KV cache fragmentation and the resulting p95/p99 latency spikes under bursty traffic and mixed sequence-length workloads.

Context / why now
- We’ve seen allocator churn + fragmentation lead to bursty p95/p99 decode latency (and occasionally allocation failures/OOM risk) in a subset of hosted regions and dedicated pools.
- This project is seeded by the Feb latency incident/postmortem and multiple customer escalations tied to tail latency stability.

Goals
1) Reduce fragmentation under production-like mixes (prefill/decode interleaving, variable context lengths, multi-tenant pools).
2) Reduce KV-cache-related tail latency spikes (p95/p99) attributable to allocator search/eviction/reallocation.
3) Define an explicit scheduler ↔ KV cache contract for eviction/pressure signals (fairness + backpressure + overload behavior).
4) Add observability to make this measurable and safe to roll out (allocator/fragmentation metrics, compaction cost, per-request attribution).
5) Ship behind a runtime flag with staged canary (by region/pool) and clear rollback triggers.

Non-goals
- Full rewrite of attention cache subsystem or changes to model semantics.
- Offline defrag across device resets; focus is online compaction/eviction during runtime.
- Any major Console UX initiative beyond required dashboard panels/alerts.

Primary deliverables
- Design doc + ADRs (block size/move semantics; trigger policy/budgeting; eviction policy/scheduler contract)
- Implementation PR series (metrics → allocator abstraction → eviction → compaction engine → scheduler integration → flags)
- Perf suite additions + perf-canary gate for fragmentation-induced tails
- Dashboard + alerts + SRE runbook updates for rollout/rollback

Success metrics (initial targets; measured vs baseline + on perf-canary)
- Fragmentation: 30–50% reduction in “fragmentation ratio” in bursty-mix benchmark scenarios (exact definition in runtime architecture page).
- Tail latency: measurable p99 improvement on perf-canary (goal: >10% p99 reduction on affected scenarios) with no statistically significant median regression.
- Allocation failures: near-zero allocation failures in canary pools under expected load; alert if failure rate exceeds agreed threshold.
- Compaction overhead: compaction time/cost within configured budget; no sustained thrash (compaction-trigger oscillation).

Milestones / timeline (working plan)
Phase 0 (1–2 weeks)
- Incident/data review + instrumentation plan + baseline fragmentation benchmarks
- Draft design + ADRs for block size/move semantics + triggers/budgets + eviction contract

Phase 1 (2–4 weeks)
- Implement allocator refactor + metrics + feature flag scaffolding
- Eviction strategy v1 integrated (correctness + fairness constraints)

Phase 2 (2–3 weeks)
- Scheduler integration (cache pressure/backpressure signals) + compaction triggers/budget enforcement
- Regression suite + stress tests under concurrent prefill/decode

Phase 3 (1–2 weeks)
- Canary rollout: 1 hosted region + 1 dedicated pool
- Dashboards/alerts live; iterate budgets/thresholds based on real traffic

Phase 4 (1–2 weeks)
- Broad rollout (staged enablement) + documentation and oncall readiness

Rollout plan (high level)
- Default OFF behind runtime flag.
- Canary enablement scoped to a single hosted region + a single dedicated pool.
- Roll forward only if: p99 improves or stays flat within tolerance, allocation failures do not increase, and median latency does not regress.
- Immediate rollback triggers: sustained p99 regression, increase in allocation failures, compaction thrash, or any correctness signals.

Notes / open questions
- Block size tradeoff: smaller blocks reduce internal fragmentation but increase metadata/lookup cost; larger blocks simplify kernels but waste memory under mixed lengths.
- Move semantics: ensure pointer/address stability for in-flight kernels; stream sync points must be explicit.
- Eviction vs prefix-cache: avoid punishing high-reuse prefixes; need a clear priority model and guardrails.
- Multi-tenant fairness: eviction must not starve low-tier tenants indefinitely; scheduler contract must specify invariants.
